courses.title: Ch 4 · Agriculture
courses.summary: Types of farming in India, the three cropping seasons, major food and non-food crops with their growing conditions and regions, and technological and institutional reforms.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish primitive subsistence, intensive subsistence, commercial and plantation farming
Learners can classify crops into rabi, kharif and zaid
Learners can state growing conditions and leading areas for major crops
Learners can explain reforms such as land reforms, Green and White Revolutions and farmer schemes

scenes.text: In Mizoram, Lalremsiami's family clears a forest patch, burns it and sows rice in the ash.
After a few years they move on and let the land recover – this is jhumming.

steps.title: Primitive subsistence farming
steps.body:
Practised on small patches with primitive tools (hoe, dao, digging sticks) and family/community labour; depends on monsoon, natural soil fertility and environmental conditions.

**Slash and burn (shifting) agriculture:** farmers clear land, grow cereals and other food crops; when fertility falls they shift to a new patch. Local names: **jhumming** (NE states – Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland), **Pamlou** (Manipur), **Dipa** (Bastar, Chhattisgarh, and Andaman & Nicobar), **Bewar/Dahiya** (MP), **Podu/Penda** (AP), **Pama Dabi/Koman/Bringa** (Odisha), **Kumari** (Western Ghats), **Valre/Waltre** (SE Rajasthan), **Khil** (Himalayan belt), **Kuruwa** (Jharkhand).

steps.title: Intensive, commercial and plantation farming
steps.body:
- **Intensive subsistence farming:** in areas of high population pressure on land; labour-intensive; high doses of biochemical inputs and irrigation. The “right of inheritance” leads to division of land into ever-smaller holdings.
- **Commercial farming:** high doses of modern inputs – HYV seeds, chemical fertilisers, insecticides and pesticides. Degree of commercialisation varies: rice is a commercial crop in **Haryana and Punjab**, but a subsistence crop in **Odisha**.
- **Plantation:** a type of commercial farming where a single crop is grown on a large area; interface of agriculture and industry; large tracts, capital-intensive inputs, migrant labour; produce used as raw material in industries. Examples: **tea, coffee, rubber, sugarcane, banana**. Tea in Assam and North Bengal; coffee in Karnataka. A well-developed network of transport and communication, processing industries and markets is needed.

steps.title: Solved example: Distinguish intensive subsistence and commercial farming (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Aim:** intensive subsistence feeds the family; commercial farming grows for sale.

**Step 2 – Inputs:** intensive subsistence = high labour, some biochemical inputs on small plots; commercial = HYV seeds, fertilisers, pesticides, machines on larger farms.

**Step 3 – Example:** rice is commercial in Punjab/Haryana but subsistence in Odisha.

steps.title: Solved example: Why is plantation farming called the interface of agriculture and industry? (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Crops are grown on large estates using capital-intensive methods and migrant labour.

**Step 2:** The entire produce is used as raw material by industries (e.g. tea processing), linking farm and factory.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Matching jhumming with MP – it is the **north-east**; Bewar/Dahiya is MP.
- Saying commercial farming is defined by crop type – it depends on **purpose and inputs** (rice can be either).

In the short summer gap, they grow watermelons – a zaid crop.

steps.title: Rabi, kharif, zaid
steps.body:
- **Rabi:** sown in winter (**October–December**) and harvested in summer (**April–June**). Crops: **wheat, barley, peas, gram, mustard**. Grown in states from Punjab, Haryana, HP, J&K, Uttarakhand to UP. Winter precipitation from **western temperate cyclones** helps; the Green Revolution in Punjab, Haryana, western UP and parts of Rajasthan boosted rabi crops.
- **Kharif:** sown with the onset of monsoon in different parts of the country and harvested in **September–October**. Crops: **paddy, maize, jowar, bajra, tur (arhar), moong, urad, cotton, jute, groundnut and soybean**. Paddy-growing regions include Assam, West Bengal, coastal Odisha, AP, Telangana, TN, Kerala, Maharashtra (Konkan) along with UP and Bihar; recently Punjab and Haryana too. In **Assam, West Bengal and Odisha, three crops of paddy** are grown: **Aus, Aman and Boro**.
- **Zaid:** a short season between rabi and kharif in summer months. Crops: **watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, vegetables, fodder crops**. **Sugarcane** takes almost a year to grow.

steps.title: Solved example: Classify: mustard, jute, cucumber, gram, soybean (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Rabi:** mustard, gram.

**Step 2 – Kharif:** jute, soybean.

**Step 3 – Zaid:** cucumber.

steps.title: Solved example: Why is rabi cultivation successful in north-west India? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Winter rain from western temperate cyclones.

**Step 2:** Irrigation from canals and tube wells (Green Revolution technology).

**Step 3:** Cool growing season and sunshine at ripening suit wheat.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling cotton a rabi crop – it is **kharif**.
- Mixing up Aus, Aman, Boro (paddy seasons in Assam/WB/Odisha) with crop names.
- Calling sugarcane a zaid crop – it takes about a **year**.

scenes.text: Ananya's lunch has rice, roti, dal and a ragi ladoo.
Each item grows in a different climate and soil across India.

steps.title: Cereals
steps.body:
- **Rice:** staple for most people; India is the **second largest producer after China**. Kharif crop; needs **high temperature (above 25°C), high humidity, annual rainfall above 100 cm**; less in areas with irrigation. Grown in northern and north-eastern plains, coastal areas and deltas; canals and tube wells made it possible in Punjab, Haryana, western UP and parts of Rajasthan.
- **Wheat:** second most important cereal; main food crop in north and north-west. Needs a **cool growing season and bright sunshine at ripening; 50–75 cm** of evenly distributed rainfall. Two important zones: the **Ganga–Satluj plains** in the north-west and the **black soil region of the Deccan**. Major states: Punjab, Haryana, UP, MP, Bihar, Rajasthan.
- **Millets (coarse grains, very high nutritional value):** **jowar** (third most important food crop by area and production; rain-fed, mostly in moist areas needing little irrigation; Maharashtra largest producer, followed by Karnataka, AP, MP); **bajra** (sandy and shallow black soils; Rajasthan largest producer, followed by UP, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Haryana); **ragi** (dry regions; red, black, sandy, loamy and shallow black soils; very rich in iron, calcium, other micronutrients and roughage; Karnataka largest, followed by TN; also HP, Uttarakhand, Sikkim, Jharkhand, Arunachal).
- **Maize:** food and fodder; kharif crop needing **21–27°C** and old alluvial soil; in some states (e.g. Bihar) also grown in rabi. Major states: Karnataka, MP, UP, Bihar, AP, Telangana.

steps.title: Pulses
steps.body: India is the **largest producer and consumer of pulses** in the world. They are the major source of **protein** in a vegetarian diet. Major pulses: **tur (arhar), urad, moong, masur, peas and gram**. They need less moisture and survive dry conditions. Being **leguminous**, all except arhar help restore soil fertility by **fixing nitrogen** from the air, so they are rotated with other crops. Major states: MP, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, UP, Karnataka.

steps.title: Solved example: State the geographical conditions for rice and wheat (4 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Rice:** temperature above 25°C, high humidity, rainfall above 100 cm (or irrigation); alluvial plains and deltas.

**Step 2 – Wheat:** cool growing season, bright sunshine at ripening, 50–75 cm evenly distributed rainfall.

**Step 3 – Regions:** rice – northern/NE plains, coastal deltas; wheat – Ganga–Satluj plains and black soil Deccan.

steps.title: Solved example: Why are pulses grown in rotation with other crops? (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Pulses are leguminous – they fix atmospheric nitrogen in the soil (except arhar).

**Step 2:** This restores soil fertility for the next crop, reducing fertiliser needs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying India is the largest producer of rice – it is **second after China**.
- Saying ragi is grown mainly in Punjab – **Karnataka** is the largest producer.
- Mixing up rainfall needs: rice >100 cm, wheat 50–75 cm.

steps.title: Sugarcane, oilseeds, tea, coffee, horticulture
steps.body:
- **Sugarcane:** tropical and subtropical; hot and humid climate, **21–27°C**, **75–100 cm** rain; irrigation needed in low-rainfall areas. India is the **second largest producer after Brazil**. Source of sugar, gur, khandsari, molasses. Major states: UP, Maharashtra, Karnataka, TN, AP, Telangana, Bihar, Punjab, Haryana.
- **Oilseeds:** groundnut (kharif; major oilseed), mustard (rabi), sesamum (kharif in north, rabi in south), castor (both), linseed, coconut, soybean, cotton seeds, sunflower. Used for cooking and as raw material for soap, cosmetics and ointments.
- **Tea:** plantation crop introduced by the British. Grows in tropical and subtropical climates on **deep, fertile, well-drained soil rich in humus and organic matter**; warm and moist frost-free climate throughout the year; frequent showers evenly distributed. Labour-intensive. Major states: **Assam, hills of Darjeeling and Jalpaiguri (WB), TN, Kerala**; also HP, Uttarakhand, Meghalaya, AP, Tripura.
- **Coffee:** Indian coffee is known for good quality; the **Arabica** variety was initially brought from **Yemen** and first grown in the **Baba Budan Hills**. Cultivation is confined to the **Nilgiri** in Karnataka, Kerala and TN.
- **Horticulture:** India produces tropical and temperate fruits – mangoes (Maharashtra, AP, Telangana, UP, WB), oranges (Nagpur, Cherrapunji), bananas (Kerala, Mizoram, Maharashtra, TN), lichi and guava (UP, Bihar), pineapples (Meghalaya), grapes (AP, Telangana, Maharashtra), apples, pears, apricots and walnuts (J&K, HP).

steps.title: Rubber and fibres
steps.body:
- **Rubber:** equatorial crop; also grown in tropical and subtropical areas; moist and humid climate, **rainfall over 200 cm**, temperature above 25°C. Mainly in **Kerala, TN, Karnataka, Andaman & Nicobar, Garo hills of Meghalaya**.
- **Fibre crops:** cotton, jute, hemp and natural silk. Silk comes from cocoons of silkworms fed on mulberry leaves – rearing silkworms is **sericulture**.
- **Cotton:** India is believed to be the original home of cotton. Grows well in the drier parts of the **black cotton soil of the Deccan**; needs high temperature, light rainfall or irrigation, **210 frost-free days** and bright sunshine; kharif crop, 6–8 months to mature. Major states: Maharashtra, Gujarat, MP, Karnataka, AP, Telangana, TN, Punjab, Haryana, UP.
- **Jute:** the “**golden fibre**”; grows on well-drained fertile soils of flood plains where soils are renewed every year; high temperature needed. Major states: **West Bengal, Bihar, Assam, Odisha, Meghalaya**. Used for gunny bags, mats, ropes, yarn, carpets; losing market to synthetic fibres, especially nylon.

steps.title: Solved example: Compare the conditions for tea and coffee (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Tea:** warm, moist, frost-free climate all year; frequent evenly distributed showers; deep fertile humus-rich well-drained soil; labour-intensive.

**Step 2 – Coffee:** grown on hill slopes – Arabica from Yemen, first in Baba Budan Hills; Nilgiri hills of Karnataka, Kerala, TN.

**Step 3 – Regions:** tea – Assam, Darjeeling; coffee – Karnataka mainly.

steps.title: Solved example: Why is jute called the golden fibre and why is it declining? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Name:** golden colour and high value for the economy of Bengal.

**Step 2 – Conditions:** flood-plain soils renewed yearly; high temperature.

**Step 3 – Decline:** high cost and competition from synthetic fibres, especially nylon.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying rubber needs low rainfall – it needs **over 200 cm**.
- Writing that India is the largest sugarcane producer – it is **second after Brazil**.
- Saying coffee first came from Ethiopia per NCERT – NCERT says Arabica was brought from **Yemen**.

steps.title: Reforms after Independence
steps.body:
- **Land reforms** were a main focus of the First Five Year Plan: collectivisation, consolidation of holdings, cooperation and abolition of **zamindari**. Implementation lagged.
- **Green Revolution** (1960s–70s, based on package technology – HYV seeds, fertilisers, irrigation) and **White Revolution** (**Operation Flood**) were strategies to improve agriculture; but they concentrated development in a few selected areas.
- In the 1980s and 1990s a comprehensive land development programme included institutional and technical reforms: crop insurance against drought, flood, cyclone, fire and disease; **Grameen banks**, cooperative societies and banks for loans at lower interest rates.
- **Kisan Credit Card (KCC)** and **Personal Accident Insurance Scheme (PAIS)**; special weather bulletins and agricultural programmes on radio and TV; **Minimum Support Price (MSP)**, remunerative and procurement prices announced by the government to check exploitation by speculators and middlemen.
- **Bhoodan–Gramdan:** Vinoba Bhave, a spiritual heir of Gandhi, walked across the country. At Pochampalli (Andhra Pradesh) some landless villagers asked for land; Shri Ram Chandra Reddy offered **80 acres** – the start of Bhoodan. Some zamindars offered whole villages (**Gramdan**). Some landowners donated partly out of fear of land ceiling laws.

steps.title: Solved example: How does MSP help farmers? (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** The government announces a minimum price before sowing at which it will buy crops.

**Step 2:** This protects farmers from price crashes and exploitation by middlemen and speculators.

steps.title: Solved example: Why was the Green Revolution criticised? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Regional concentration:** benefits went mainly to Punjab, Haryana, western UP.

**Step 2 – Ecological costs:** heavy fertiliser and water use led to soil degradation and falling water tables.

**Step 3 – Inequality:** richer farmers with irrigation gained more.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Linking Operation Flood with crops – it is the **White Revolution (milk)**.
- Writing that Bhoodan was government legislation – it was a **voluntary movement** led by Vinoba Bhave.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Minerals and Energy Resources
courses.summary: What minerals are and how they occur, ferrous, non-ferrous and non-metallic minerals of India and their belts, hazards and conservation of minerals, and conventional and non-conventional sources of energy.
outcomes: Learners can describe modes of occurrence of minerals with examples
Learners can locate major iron ore belts and other mineral regions
Learners can compare types of coal and locate petroleum and gas fields
Learners can explain non-conventional energy sources and conservation of energy

scenes.text: In Jowai and Cherrapunji (Meghalaya), coal was once dug by family members through long narrow tunnels – "rat-hole" mining.
Geologists explain that minerals occur in many different ways in rocks.

steps.title: What is a mineral?
steps.body: Geologists define a mineral as a **homogeneous, naturally occurring substance with a definable internal structure**. Minerals are found in varied forms – from the hardest diamond to the softest talc. Rocks are combinations of homogeneous substances called minerals. Minerals are usually found in **ores** – accumulations of a mineral mixed with other elements.

steps.title: Modes of occurrence
steps.body:
- **Igneous and metamorphic rocks:** in cracks, crevices, faults or joints. Smaller occurrences are **veins**, larger are **lodes**. Formed when minerals in liquid/molten/gaseous form are forced upward. Examples: **tin, copper, zinc, lead**.
- **Sedimentary rocks:** in **beds or layers**, formed by deposition and accumulation in horizontal strata – **coal, some iron ore** (long heat and pressure); **gypsum, potash salt, sodium salt** (evaporation in arid regions).
- **Decomposition of surface rocks:** soluble constituents removed, leaving a residual mass of weathered material containing ores – **bauxite**.
- **Alluvial deposits in sands of valley floors and the base of hills** – **placer deposits** of minerals not corroded by water: **gold, silver, tin, platinum**.
- **Ocean waters:** most minerals are too diffused, but **common salt, magnesium and bromine** are largely derived from ocean waters. Ocean beds are rich in manganese nodules.

steps.title: Solved example: Name the mode of occurrence: bauxite, gold in river sand, gypsum (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Bauxite – decomposition of surface rocks (residual mass).

**Step 2:** Gold in river sand – alluvial / placer deposit.

**Step 3:** Gypsum – sedimentary beds formed by evaporation in arid regions.

steps.title: Solved example: Distinguish veins and lodes (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Both occur in cracks/faults of igneous and metamorphic rocks.

**Step 2:** Veins are smaller occurrences; lodes are larger ones (e.g. tin, copper, zinc, lead).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling all rocks minerals – rocks are **combinations** of minerals.
- Putting bauxite in placer deposits – it forms from **decomposition of surface rocks**.
- Saying salt is mined only from rocks – common salt is largely from **ocean water**.

scenes.text: At Kudremukh in Karnataka, iron ore was once sent as slurry through a pipeline to the port near Mangaluru.
Other ore travels by rail to Visakhapatnam and is exported to Japan and South Korea.

steps.title: Ferrous minerals: iron and manganese
steps.body:
**Ferrous minerals** account for about three-fourths of the total value of metallic mineral production.

- **Iron ore:** **magnetite** is the finest iron ore with very high iron content of **up to 70%**, with excellent magnetic qualities, valuable in the electrical industry; **haematite** is the most important industrial iron ore by quantity used, with **50–60%** iron.
- **Iron ore belts:** (1) **Odisha–Jharkhand belt** – high-grade haematite at Badampahar mines (Mayurbhanj and Kendujhar districts, Odisha); in Singhbhum (Jharkhand) haematite mined at Gua and Noamundi. (2) **Durg–Bastar–Chandrapur belt** (Chhattisgarh and Maharashtra) – very high-grade haematite in the **Bailadila** range (hill resembles the hump of an ox) – **14 deposits**; exported to **Japan and South Korea via Visakhapatnam port**. (3) **Ballari–Chitradurga–Chikkamagaluru–Tumakuru belt** (Karnataka) – **Kudremukh** in the Western Ghats is said to be one of the largest in the world; ore transported as slurry through a pipeline to a port near Mangaluru. (4) **Maharashtra–Goa belt** – ore not very high quality but efficiently exploited; exported through **Marmagao port**.
- **Manganese:** used in manufacturing steel and ferro-manganese alloy; nearly **10 kg of manganese** is required to make **one tonne of steel**; also for bleaching powder, insecticides and paints.

steps.title: Non-ferrous and non-metallic minerals
steps.body:
- **Copper:** malleable, ductile, good conductor – electrical cables, electronics, chemicals. **Balaghat mines (MP), Khetri mines (Rajasthan), Singhbhum (Jharkhand)**.
- **Bauxite:** aluminium is obtained from bauxite (clay-like substance, from decomposition of rocks rich in aluminium silicates). Light, good conductor, malleable. Deposits mainly in the **Amarkantak plateau, Maikal hills and the plateau region of Bilaspur–Katni**. **Odisha** was the largest bauxite-producing state; **Panchpatmali** deposits in **Koraput** district.
- **Mica:** made of a series of plates or leaves; splits easily into thin sheets; excellent di-electric strength, low power loss, insulating properties – used in electric and electronic industries. Found on the northern edge of the **Chota Nagpur plateau**; **Koderma–Gaya–Hazaribagh belt (Jharkhand)** is a leading producer; also **Ajmer (Rajasthan)** and **Nellore (AP)**.
- **Rock minerals – limestone:** found with rocks of calcium carbonate or calcium and magnesium carbonates; basic raw material for the **cement industry** and essential for smelting iron ore in blast furnaces.

**Hazards of mining:** dust and noxious fumes inhaled by miners make them vulnerable to **pulmonary diseases**; risk of collapsing roofs, inundation and fires in coal mines; water sources contaminated; dumping of waste and slurry degrades land and soil and increases stream and river pollution.

**Conservation:** minerals are finite and non-renewable; their replenishment is extremely slow. Use them in a planned and sustainable manner; improved technologies to use low-grade ores; **recycling of metals, using scrap metals and substitutes**.

steps.title: Solved example: Compare magnetite and haematite (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Magnetite:** finest iron ore, up to 70% iron, magnetic properties useful for electrical industry.

**Step 2 – Haematite:** most important industrial ore by quantity used; 50–60% iron.

steps.title: Solved example: Describe the Durg–Bastar–Chandrapur belt (3 marks)

steps.title: Coal
steps.body:
Coal is the most abundantly available fossil fuel in India and provides a substantial part of the nation's energy needs. It is formed from the compression of plant material over millions of years.

- **Peat:** decaying plants in swamps; low carbon, high moisture, low heating capacity.
- **Lignite:** low-grade **brown coal**, soft with high moisture content; main reserves at **Neyveli (Tamil Nadu)**; used for electricity generation.
- **Bituminous:** coal buried deep and subjected to increased temperatures; most popular in commercial use; **metallurgical coal** is high-grade bituminous coal of special value for smelting iron in blast furnaces.
- **Anthracite:** **highest quality hard coal**.

**Geological ages:** **Gondwana** coal (a little over **200 million years** old) – major resources in the **Damodar valley** (West Bengal–Jharkhand): **Jharia, Raniganj, Bokaro**; also Godavari, Mahanadi, Son and Wardha valleys. **Tertiary** coal (about 55 million years old) in north-eastern states – Meghalaya, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland. Coal is bulky and loses weight on use, so heavy industries and thermal power stations are located on or near coalfields.

steps.title: Petroleum, natural gas, electricity
steps.body:
- **Petroleum:** provides fuel for heat and lighting, lubricants for machinery, and raw materials for manufacturing; refineries are a nodal industry for synthetic textiles, fertilisers and chemicals. Most occurrences are associated with **anticlines and fault traps** in rock formations of the tertiary age. About **63%** of India's petroleum production came from **Mumbai High**, **18%** from **Gujarat** and **16%** from **Assam** (NCERT figures). **Ankeleshwar** is the most important field of Gujarat. Assam is the oldest oil-producing state; **Digboi, Naharkatiya and Moran-Hugrijan** are important fields.
- **Natural gas:** clean energy resource; used as a source of energy and as an industrial raw material in the petrochemical industry. Large reserves in the **Krishna–Godavari basin**; also Mumbai High and allied fields, Gulf of Khambhat and Andaman & Nicobar islands. The **Hazira–Vijaipur–Jagdishpur (HVJ)** pipeline links Mumbai High and Bassein with fertiliser, power and industrial complexes in western and northern India. **CNG** is increasingly used for vehicles.
- **Electricity:** generated by running water driving turbines (**hydro electricity** – renewable; e.g. Bhakra Nangal, Damodar Valley Corporation, Kopili Hydel Project) and by burning coal, petroleum and natural gas (**thermal power** – non-renewable; over 300 thermal plants per NCERT).

steps.title: Non-conventional sources
steps.body:
Growing consumption of energy has made India dependent on coal, oil and gas; rising prices and environmental problems have increased the need for sustainable sources.

- **Nuclear/atomic energy:** obtained by altering the structure of atoms; **uranium and thorium** from Jharkhand and the Aravalli ranges of Rajasthan; **monazite sands of Kerala** are rich in thorium.
- **Solar energy:** photovoltaic technology converts sunlight into electricity; a large solar power plant is at **Madhapur, near Bhuj**, where solar energy is used to **sterilise milk cans**. Solar energy will reduce dependence on firewood and dung cakes in rural areas.
- **Wind power:** India is a significant wind-power producer. The largest wind farm cluster is from **Nagercoil to Madurai** in Tamil Nadu; also AP, Karnataka, Gujarat, Kerala, Maharashtra and Lakshadweep. **Nagercoil and Jaisalmer** are well known for effective use of wind energy.
- **Biogas:** shrubs, farm waste, animal and human waste produce biogas; higher thermal efficiency than kerosene, dung cake and charcoal. **Gobar gas plants** provide energy and improved quality manure, preventing loss of trees and manure from burning cow dung.
- **Tidal energy:** oceanic tides generate electricity – floodgate dams built across inlets. In India the **Gulf of Khambhat, Gulf of Kachchh** in Gujarat and the **Gangetic delta in the Sundarbans** (West Bengal) offer ideal conditions.
- **Geothermal energy:** heat from the interior of the Earth; hot springs. Two experimental projects: **Parvati valley near Manikarn (HP)** and **Puga valley (Ladakh)**.

steps.title: Conserving energy
steps.body: Energy is a basic requirement for economic development. We must adopt a cautious approach for judicious use of limited energy resources: use **public transport** instead of individual vehicles; **switch off electricity** when not in use; use **power-saving devices**; use non-conventional sources of energy. “**Energy saved is energy produced.**”

steps.title: Why manufacturing matters
Location and classification
steps.body:
**Location factors:** raw material, labour, capital, power, market and infrastructure (banking, insurance, transport). Industrialisation and urbanisation go hand in hand; cities provide markets and services. **Agglomeration economies**: many industries cluster around an urban centre to share its advantages.

**Classification:**
- **Source of raw material:** agro-based (cotton, woollen, jute, silk textiles, rubber, sugar, tea, coffee, edible oil) and mineral-based (iron and steel, cement, aluminium, machine tools, petrochemicals).
- **Prime role:** **basic or key industries** supply products or raw materials to manufacture other goods (iron and steel, copper smelting, aluminium smelting); **consumer industries** produce goods for direct use (sugar, toothpaste, paper, sewing machines, fans).
- **Capital investment:** small-scale vs large-scale (defined by the maximum investment allowed on assets).
- **Ownership:** **public sector** (BHEL, SAIL), **private sector** (TISCO, Bajaj Auto Ltd, Dabur Industries), **joint sector** (Oil India Ltd – jointly public and private), **cooperative sector** (sugar industry in Maharashtra, coir industry in Kerala).
- **Bulk and weight of raw material and finished goods:** heavy industries (iron and steel) and light industries (electrical goods).

steps.title: Textile industry
steps.body:
The textile industry occupies a unique position: it contributes significantly to industrial production, employment and foreign exchange. It is the **only industry in the country which is self-reliant and complete in the value chain**, i.e. from raw material to the highest value-added products.

- **Cotton textiles:** in ancient India produced by hand spinning and handloom weaving; after the 18th century power-looms came. The **first successful textile mill was established in Mumbai in 1854**. Two world wars and Swadeshi helped growth. Early mills were in the cotton-growing belt of **Maharashtra and Gujarat** – availability of raw cotton, market, transport, ports, labour, moist climate. **Spinning** is centralised in Maharashtra, Gujarat and Tamil Nadu; **weaving** is highly decentralised (handloom, powerloom, mills). India has a large share in world trade of cotton yarn. Problems: power supply erratic, machinery needs upgrading, low output of labour, stiff competition with synthetic fibre industry.
- **Jute textiles:** India is the **largest producer of raw jute and jute goods** and the second largest exporter after **Bangladesh**. The **first jute mill** was set up near Kolkata at **Rishra** – the Geography textbook gives **1859** (the History textbook gives 1855 for the first jute mill in Bengal). Most mills are in West Bengal along the banks of the **Hugli** river in a narrow belt. Factors: proximity of jute-producing areas, inexpensive water transport, railways, roadways and waterways, abundant water for processing, cheap labour from WB and adjoining states, Kolkata as a large urban centre for banking, insurance and port. Challenges: stiff competition from synthetic substitutes and from Bangladesh, Brazil, Philippines, Egypt and Thailand. The **National Jute Policy (2005)** aimed to increase productivity, improve quality and ensure good prices; growing global concern for eco-friendly biodegradable materials has opened up opportunities.

steps.title: Sugar industry
steps.body:
India stands **second as a world producer of sugar** but occupies the first place in the production of **gur and khandsari**. Raw material is bulky and sucrose content falls in haulage, so mills are located near cane fields. Mills are concentrated in **UP, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka, TN, AP, Gujarat, Punjab, Haryana and MP**. About 60% of mills are in UP and Bihar (NCERT figure). The industry is seasonal, so ideally suited to the **cooperative** sector.

**Shift to southern and western states (especially Maharashtra):** cane there has **higher sucrose content**; **cooler climate** ensures a **longer crushing season**; **cooperatives are more successful** in these states.

Challenges: seasonal nature, old and inefficient methods, transport delays in reaching factories, need to maximise use of **bagasse**.

steps.title: Iron and steel; aluminium
steps.body:
- **Iron and steel** is a **basic** industry – all other industries (heavy, medium, light) depend on it for machinery – and a **heavy** industry because all raw materials and finished goods are heavy and bulky. Raw materials: iron ore, coking coal and limestone in a ratio of approximately **4:2:1**; some manganese to harden steel. Products: steel used in other industries. Types: **integrated steel plants** (large, handle everything under one roof from raw material to steel making, rolling and shaping) and **mini steel plants** (smaller, electric furnaces, use steel scrap and sponge iron, produce mild and alloy steel). Most public sector undertakings market steel through **SAIL**; TISCO markets through Tata Steel. **Chota Nagpur plateau** region has the maximum concentration – low cost of iron ore, high-grade raw materials in proximity, cheap labour, vast growth potential in the home market. India ranks among the world's top crude steel producers but per capita consumption is low. Issues: high costs and limited availability of coking coal, lower productivity of labour, irregular supply of energy, poor infrastructure.
- **Aluminium smelting** is the second most important metallurgical industry in India. Aluminium is light, resistant to corrosion, a good conductor of heat, malleable and becomes strong when mixed with other metals – used for aircraft, utensils and wires. Raw material: **bauxite** (dark reddish rock). Plants in Odisha, West Bengal, Kerala, UP, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra and TN. Location factors: **regular supply of electricity** and an assured source of raw material at minimum cost.

steps.title: Chemical, fertiliser, cement, automobile, IT
steps.body:
- **Chemical industries:** comprise large and small units; both **inorganic** (sulphuric acid for fertilisers, synthetic fibres, plastics, adhesives, paints, dyestuffs; nitric acid, alkalies, soda ash for glass, soaps, detergents, paper; caustic soda) and **organic** (petrochemicals for synthetic fibres, rubber, plastics, dyestuffs, drugs and pharmaceuticals). The chemical industry is its own largest consumer.
- **Fertiliser industry:** centred around nitrogenous fertilisers (mainly **urea**), phosphatic fertilisers, **ammonium phosphate (DAP)** and complex fertilisers. Potash is entirely imported, as India has no reserves of commercially usable potash. After the Green Revolution the industry expanded; **Gujarat, TN, UP, Punjab and Kerala** contribute half the production.
- **Cement industry:** essential for construction; requires bulky, heavy raw materials like **limestone, silica and gypsum**, plus coal, electric power and rail transport. The **first cement plant was set up in Chennai in 1904**. Decontrol of price and distribution since 1989 and other policy reforms led to rapid growth; Indian cement is exported to East Asia, Middle East, Africa and South Asia.
- **Automobile industry:** provides vehicles for quick transport of goods and passengers; liberalisation brought new and contemporary models; growth in demand. Centres around **Delhi, Gurugram, Mumbai, Pune, Chennai, Kolkata, Lucknow, Indore, Hyderabad, Jamshedpur and Bengaluru**.
- **IT and electronics:** products from transistor sets to TV, telephones, cellular telecom, pagers, telephone exchange, radar, computers. **Bengaluru** has emerged as the **electronic capital of India**; other centres Mumbai, Delhi, Hyderabad, Pune, Chennai, Kolkata, Lucknow, Coimbatore. Software technology parks provide single-window service and high-speed data communication. Major impact: employment, including a large share of women.

steps.title: Types of pollution
steps.body:
- **Air pollution:** high proportion of undesirable gases such as **sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide**; suspended particulate matter (solid and liquid). Sources: chemical and paper factories, brick kilns, refineries, smelting plants, burning of fossil fuels in big and small factories. Toxic gas leaks can be very hazardous (e.g. the Bhopal gas tragedy).
- **Water pollution:** organic and inorganic industrial effluents discharged into rivers – paper, pulp, chemical, textile and dyeing, petroleum refineries, tanneries and electroplating industries let out dyes, detergents, acids, salts and heavy metals like lead and mercury, pesticides, fertilisers, synthetic chemicals with carbon, plastics and rubber. Fly ash, phosphogypsum and iron and steel slags are main solid wastes.
- **Thermal pollution:** when hot water from factories and thermal plants is drained into rivers and ponds before cooling. Wastes from nuclear power plants and nuclear and weapon production facilities cause cancers, birth defects and miscarriages.
- **Noise pollution:** causes irritation and anger, hearing impairment, increased heart rate and blood pressure; sources: generators, exhaust fans, saws, pneumatic and electric drills.
- **Land pollution:** dumping of wastes, especially glass, harmful chemicals, industrial effluents, packaging, salts and garbage – soil becomes useless; rainwater percolates contaminants into groundwater.

steps.title: Control measures
steps.body:
- Minimise use of water by **reusing and recycling** in two or more successive stages.
- **Harvest rainwater** to meet water requirements.
- **Treat hot water and effluents** before releasing into rivers and ponds: **primary** (mechanical – screening, grinding, flocculation, sedimentation), **secondary** (biological process), **tertiary** (biological, chemical and physical processes – recycling of waste water).
- Regulate overdrawing of groundwater by industries.
- Reduce particulate matter by fitting smoke stacks with **electrostatic precipitators, fabric filters, scrubbers and inertial separators**; use oil or gas instead of coal.
- Reduce noise with silencers; redesign machinery for energy efficiency; ear plugs and earphones for workers.
- **NTPC** is a good example: optimum utilisation of equipment, minimising waste generation by maximising ash utilisation, green belts, reducing pollution through ash pond management and ash water recycling systems, ecological monitoring and reviews.

steps.title: Solved example: List three stages of effluent treatment (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Primary:** mechanical means – screening, grinding, flocculation, sedimentation.

**Step 2 – Secondary:** biological process.

**Step 3 – Tertiary:** biological, chemical and physical processes; involves recycling of waste water.

**Step 2:** Minimising waste by maximising ash utilisation; ash pond management and ash water recycling.

**Step 3:** Green belts for nurturing ecological balance; ecological monitoring.

steps.title: Why roads, and types of roads
steps.body:
India has one of the largest road networks in the world. Roads score over railways because: construction cost is much lower; they can traverse dissected and undulating topography and steep gradients (e.g. the Himalayas); they negotiate higher gradients; they are economical for a few persons and small loads over short distances; they provide **door-to-door service** so loading/unloading costs are lower; and they feed other modes (link railway stations, air and sea ports).

**Classification by capacity:**
- **Golden Quadrilateral Super Highways:** six-lane super highways connecting **Delhi–Kolkata–Chennai–Mumbai–Delhi**. The **North–South corridor** links **Srinagar (J&K) and Kanyakumari (TN)**; the **East–West corridor** links **Silchar (Assam) and Porbandar (Gujarat)**. The major objective is to reduce time and distance between mega cities. Implemented by the **National Highway Authority of India (NHAI)**.
- **National Highways:** link extreme parts of the country; primary road systems laid and maintained by the **Central Public Works Department (CPWD)**. Many run in north–south and east–west directions.
- **State Highways:** link a state capital with district headquarters; built and maintained by the State **Public Works Department (PWD)**.
- **District Roads:** connect district headquarters with other places in the district; maintained by the **Zila Parishad**.
- **Other Roads:** rural roads linking villages with towns; special impetus under the **Pradhan Mantri Grameen Sadak Yojana** – every village linked to a major town by an all-season motorable road.
- **Border Roads:** the **Border Roads Organisation** (established **1960**) constructs strategic roads in northern and north-eastern border areas, improving accessibility in difficult terrain.

Roads are also classified by material: metalled (cement, concrete, bitumen) and unmetalled.

steps.title: Road density and problems
steps.body: **Road density** = length of roads per 100 sq km of area. It is low in hilly, desert and remote regions (e.g. J&K) and high in plains (e.g. Kerala). Problems: road network inadequate for traffic volume; about half the roads are unmetalled, limiting use in rainy season; National Highways are inadequate, roads are congested in cities, and most bridges and culverts are old and narrow.

steps.title: Solved example: Why are roads more useful than railways in some situations? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Cost:** construction cost is much lower.

**Step 2 – Terrain:** roads can cross undulating, hilly terrain where railways cannot easily go.

**Step 3 – Service:** door-to-door delivery, economical for small loads and short distances; they also feed railways and ports.

steps.title: Solved example: Who builds which road? (4 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Golden Quadrilateral and corridors – NHAI.

**Step 2:** National Highways – CPWD.

**Step 3:** State Highways – State PWD; District roads – Zila Parishad.

**Step 4:** Border roads – Border Roads Organisation (1960).

- Saying NHAI maintains state highways – those are **State PWD**.
- Defining road density per 1,000 sq km – it is **per 100 sq km**.

steps.title: Railways
steps.body:
Railways are the principal mode of transport for freight and passengers in India; they also make it possible to conduct multiple activities like business, sightseeing and pilgrimage, and carry goods over long distances. The first train ran from **Bombay to Thane in 1853**, covering **34 km**. Indian Railways is reorganised into **zones**.

**Factors in distribution:** physiographic, economic and administrative.
- **Northern plains** – vast level land, high population density and rich agricultural resources favour railways (but numerous rivers need bridges).
- **Peninsular plateau** – railways pass through low hills, gaps or tunnels.
- **Himalayan mountains** – unfavourable due to high relief, sparse population and lack of economic opportunity.
- **Western Rajasthan** sandy plains, swamps of Gujarat, forested Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Jharkhand are difficult.
- The **Konkan railway** along the west coast made movement easier; it faced problems like sinking of track and landslides.

**Gauges:** broad gauge (1.676 m), metre gauge (1 m), narrow gauge (0.762 m and 0.610 m).

**Problems:** many passengers travel without tickets; thefts and damage to railway property; people stop trains and pull chains unnecessarily, causing heavy damage and delays.

steps.title: Pipelines
steps.body:
Pipelines are a new arrival on India's transport map. Earlier they carried water to cities and industries; now they transport **crude oil, petroleum products and natural gas** from oil and gas fields to refineries, fertiliser factories and big thermal power plants. Solids can be carried in **slurry** form. Refineries at **Barauni, Mathura, Panipat** and gas-based fertiliser plants could be located inland because of pipelines. Initial cost is high but running costs are minimal; they rule out transhipment losses and delays.

**Three important networks:**
1. From oil fields in **upper Assam to Kanpur (UP)** via Guwahati, Barauni and Allahabad (Prayagraj), with branches from Barauni to Haldia via Rajbandh, Rajbandh to Maurigram and Guwahati to Siliguri.
2. From **Salaya (Gujarat) to Jalandhar (Punjab)** via Viramgam, Mathura, Delhi and Sonipat, with branches to Koyali (near Vadodara) and other places.
3. **Gas pipeline from Hazira (Gujarat) to Jagdishpur (UP)** via Vijaipur (MP) – the HVJ – with branches to Kota (Rajasthan), Shahjahanpur, Babrala and other places in UP.

steps.title: Solved example: Why is the railway network dense in the northern plains but sparse in the Himalayas? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Plains:** level land, dense population and rich agriculture make lines cheap to build and profitable.

**Step 2 – Himalayas:** high relief, sparse population and few economic opportunities make lines difficult and costly.

**Step 3 – Conclusion:** physiography and economy together decide distribution.

steps.title: Solved example: Give two advantages and one disadvantage of pipelines (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Advantages:** minimal running cost; no transhipment losses or delays; allow inland refineries (Mathura, Panipat).

**Step 2 – Disadvantage:** high initial cost of laying pipelines.

- Saying HVJ carries crude oil – it carries **gas**.
- Confusing broad gauge (1.676 m) with metre gauge (1 m).

steps.title: Waterways
steps.body:
Waterways are the **cheapest means of transport**, most suitable for heavy and bulky goods; fuel-efficient and environment-friendly. India has inland navigation waterways of about 14,500 km (NCERT figure).

**National Waterways (NCERT):**
- **NW-1:** the **Ganga** between **Allahabad (Prayagraj) and Haldia** (1,620 km).
- **NW-2:** the **Brahmaputra** between **Sadiya and Dhubri** (891 km).
- **NW-3:** the **West-Coast Canal** in Kerala (**Kottapuram–Kollam**, Udyogamandal and Champakkara canals – 205 km).
- NW-4 (specified stretches of the Godavari and Krishna with Kakinada–Puducherry canal) and NW-5 (specified stretches of Brahmani with Matai river, delta channels of Mahanadi and Brahmani and East Coast Canal).

Other inland waterways: Mandavi, Zuari and Cumberjua, Sunderbans, Barak and Kerala backwaters.

steps.title: Major sea ports
steps.body:
About 95% of India's foreign trade by volume moves through ocean routes (NCERT figure). India has **12 major** and about 200 notified non-major ports.

- **Kandla (Kachchh)** – first port developed soon after Independence to ease the volume of trade on Mumbai port after the loss of Karachi to Pakistan; a **tidal port**; caters to exports and imports of highly productive granary and industrial belts of J&K, HP, Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and Gujarat. (Renamed **Deendayal Port**.)
- **Mumbai** – the biggest port with a spacious natural and well-sheltered harbour. **Jawaharlal Nehru Port** was planned to decongest Mumbai and serve as a hub port.
- **Marmagao (Goa)** – premier **iron ore exporting** port, accounting for about 50% of India's iron ore export.
- **New Mangalore (Karnataka)** – exports iron ore concentrates from Kudremukh mines.
- **Kochi** – extreme south-western port at the entrance of a **lagoon** with a natural harbour.
- **Tuticorin (Tamil Nadu)** – extreme south-east; natural harbour and rich hinterland; trade with Sri Lanka, Maldives and coastal regions of India.
- **Chennai** – one of the **oldest artificial ports**; second to Mumbai in volume of trade and cargo.
- **Visakhapatnam** – the **deepest landlocked and well-protected port**; originally conceived as an outlet for iron ore exports.
- **Paradip (Odisha)** – specialises in export of iron ore.
- **Kolkata** – an **inland riverine port** serving a large and rich hinterland of the Ganga–Brahmaputra basin; a tidal port requiring constant dredging of the Hugli. **Haldia** was developed as a subsidiary port to relieve pressure on Kolkata.

**Airways:** the fastest, most comfortable and prestigious mode; can cover very difficult terrain – high mountains, dreary deserts, dense forests and long oceanic stretches – with great ease. Air travel in the north-east has a special provision for local people because of difficult terrain. Air transport was nationalised in 1953. **Air India** provides domestic and international services. **Pawan Hans Helicopters Ltd** provides helicopter services to ONGC in its offshore operations, to inaccessible areas and difficult terrains like the north-eastern states and interior parts of J&K, HP and Uttarakhand. Air travel is not within reach of common people.

**Step 2:** Kandla (Kachchh) was developed as a tidal port to handle trade of the north-western granary and industrial belt.

**Step 2 – Visakhapatnam:** deepest landlocked and well-protected port.

**Step 3 – Common role:** both serve rich hinterlands on the east coast.

scenes.text: Aditi posts a letter by speed post and wonders how mail moves so fast.
Her economics teacher talks about India's exports and imports – the balance of trade.

steps.title: Communication
steps.body:
- The **Indian Postal Network** is the largest in the world. **First-class mail** (cards and envelopes) is airlifted between stations covering both land and air; **second-class mail** (book packets, registered newspapers and periodicals) is carried by surface mail (land and water transport). To facilitate quick delivery in large towns and cities, **six mail channels** were introduced: **Rajdhani Channel, Metro Channel, Green Channel, Business Channel, Bulk Mail Channel and Periodical Channel**.
- India has one of the largest **telecom networks** in Asia; integration of STD with space communication technology; uniform STD rates for the whole country.
- **Mass communication** provides entertainment and awareness about national programmes and policies: **All India Radio (Akashwani)** broadcasts in national, regional and local languages; **Doordarshan**, the national television channel, is one of the largest terrestrial networks in the world. India publishes a large number of newspapers and periodicals; India is the largest producer of feature films in the world (NCERT). The **Central Board of Film Certification** is the authority to certify Indian and foreign films.

steps.title: International trade and tourism
steps.body:
- Exchange of goods among people, states and countries is **trade**; the market is the place where exchanges occur. Trade between two countries is international trade, through sea, air or land routes. Advancement of international trade is an index of economic prosperity; it is the economic barometer of a country.
- **Balance of trade:** the difference between a country's exports and imports. If exports exceed imports, it is a **favourable** balance of trade; if imports exceed exports, it is **unfavourable**.
- India's exports include agricultural and allied products, ores and minerals, gems and jewellery, chemicals, engineering goods and petroleum products; imports include petroleum and crude products, gems, chemicals, base metals, electronic items, machinery and fertilisers. India has emerged as a software giant earning foreign exchange through IT.
- **Tourism** has grown substantially: it promotes national integration, supports local handicrafts and cultural pursuits, helps develop international understanding of our culture and heritage, and earns foreign exchange. Foreign tourists visit for heritage, eco, adventure, cultural, medical and business tourism.

steps.title: Solved example: India's exports are ₹35 lakh crore and imports ₹55 lakh crore. Find the balance of trade and its type (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Formula:** balance of trade = exports − imports.

**Step 2 – Calculate:** 35 − 55 = −₹20 lakh crore.

**Step 3 – Type:** imports exceed exports → **unfavourable** balance of trade (trade deficit).

steps.title: Solved example: How does tourism help the nation? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Earns foreign exchange and creates jobs.

**Step 2:** Promotes national integration and supports local handicrafts and culture.

**Step 3:** Builds international understanding of India's heritage.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying first-class mail goes by surface – it is **airlifted**; second-class goes by surface.
- Calling a trade deficit “favourable”.
- Forgetting the six mail channels (often asked as a list).

courses.title: Ch 1 · Power Sharing
courses.summary: Two stories – Belgium and Sri Lanka – show why sharing power reduces conflict and deepens democracy; then the forms power sharing takes in modern democracies.
outcomes: Learners can compare how Belgium and Sri Lanka handled ethnic diversity
Learners can give prudential and moral reasons for power sharing
Learners can identify horizontal, vertical, social-group and party-level forms of power sharing

scenes.text: Belgium, a small European country, has Dutch, French and German speakers. It chose to share power.
Sri Lanka chose majority dominance – and paid for it with a long civil war.

steps.title: Belgium
steps.body:
Belgium is a small country in Europe with a population a little over one crore. Ethnic composition: **59%** live in the **Flemish** region and speak **Dutch**; **40%** live in **Wallonia** and speak **French**; **1%** speak **German**. In the capital **Brussels**, **80%** speak French and **20%** Dutch.

The French-speaking minority was richer and more powerful, which the Dutch-speaking majority resented after they gained education and wealth. Tensions in the 1950s–60s were sharper in Brussels (Dutch majority nationally, French majority in the capital).

**The Belgian model:** the constitution was **amended four times between 1970 and 1993**:
- The number of **Dutch and French-speaking ministers shall be equal** in the central government; some laws need majority support from each linguistic group – no single community can take decisions unilaterally.
- Many powers of the central government were given to **state governments** of the two regions; state governments are not subordinate to the central government.
- **Brussels** has a separate government with **equal representation** of both communities.
- A **community government** is elected by people of one language community – Dutch, French or German – wherever they live, with power over cultural, educational and language issues.

The model was complicated but avoided civic strife; Brussels was chosen as the headquarters of the **European Union**.

steps.title: Sri Lanka
steps.body:
Sri Lanka became independent in **1948**. Major social groups: **Sinhala speakers – 74%**; **Tamil speakers – 18%** (Sri Lankan Tamils 13% and Indian Tamils 5% – whose forefathers came as plantation workers in the colonial period). Most Sinhalas are Buddhist; most Tamils are Hindu or Muslim; about 7% are Christian.

**Majoritarianism:** the democratically elected government adopted measures to establish **Sinhala supremacy**:
- An **Act of 1956** recognised **Sinhala as the only official language**, disregarding Tamil.
- Preferential policies favoured Sinhala applicants for university positions and government jobs.
- The constitution provided that the state shall protect and foster **Buddhism**.

Tamils felt alienated. They launched parties and struggles for recognition of Tamil as an official language, regional autonomy and equality of opportunity. By the 1980s organisations demanded an independent **Tamil Eelam** in the north and east. The distrust turned into a **civil war** that ended in **2009**, causing thousands of deaths and setbacks to social, cultural and economic life.

steps.title: Solved example: Contrast the approaches of Belgium and Sri Lanka (4 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Belgium:** recognised regional and cultural differences; equal ministers; strong state governments; special Brussels government; community government – **accommodation**.

**Step 2 – Sri Lanka:** majority community imposed its will – Sinhala-only Act (1956), preferential policies, state protection of Buddhism – **majoritarianism**.

**Step 3 – Results:** Belgium kept unity and avoided civil war; Sri Lanka suffered a civil war until 2009.

**Step 4 – Lesson:** accommodation strengthens unity; majoritarianism undermines it.

steps.title: Solved example: Why was Brussels a special problem? (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Dutch speakers were a national majority but a minority (20%) in Brussels, where French speakers were 80%.

**Step 2:** So each community could feel threatened; Belgium gave Brussels a separate government with equal representation.

- Saying the Sinhala-only Act was passed in 1948 – it was **1956**.
- Calling Belgium's community government a regional government – it is elected by **language community**, wherever members live.

steps.title: Two sets of reasons
steps.body:
- **Prudential reasons** (careful calculation of gains and losses): power sharing **reduces the possibility of conflict** between social groups. Social conflict often leads to violence and political instability, so sharing power ensures stability. Imposing the will of the majority may look attractive in the short run but undermines unity in the long run (Sri Lanka).
- **Moral reasons** (intrinsic worth): power sharing is the **very spirit of democracy**. A democratic rule involves sharing power with those affected by its exercise and who live with its effects. People have a right to be consulted on how they are governed. A legitimate government is one where citizens, through participation, acquire a stake in the system.

steps.title: Solved example: Distinguish prudential and moral reasons (3 marks)

steps.title: Four forms
steps.body:
1. **Horizontal distribution** – among organs of government: **legislature, executive and judiciary**, placed at the same level. Each organ checks the others – a system of **checks and balances** (ministers are accountable to Parliament; judges are appointed by the executive but can check the executive and laws made by the legislature).
2. **Vertical distribution** – among governments at different levels: a general government for the entire country (**Union/central/federal government**) and governments at the provincial or regional level (state governments); also local government (municipality, panchayat). The constitution lays down the powers of each.
3. **Among social groups** – religious and linguistic groups: e.g. **community government** in Belgium; in India, **reserved constituencies** in legislatures and Parliament for socially weaker sections and women.
4. **Among political parties, pressure groups and movements** – competition among parties ensures power does not stay in one hand; **coalition governments** share power among parties; interest groups (traders, businessmen, industrialists, farmers, industrial workers) influence decisions through participation in committees or pressure.

courses.summary: What makes a country federal, coming-together and holding-together federations, how India's Constitution divides power through three lists, how federalism is practised (linguistic states, language policy, centre–state relations) and decentralisation through panchayats and municipalities.

steps.title: Federalism and its features
steps.body:
**Federalism** is a system of government in which power is divided between a central authority and various constituent units. Usually there are two levels: one for the entire country (common national interest) and others at the level of provinces or states (day-to-day administration). In a **unitary** system there is one level of government, or sub-units are subordinate to the centre (the central government can pass orders to provincial/local governments).

**Key features:**
1. Two or more levels (tiers) of government.
2. Different tiers govern the same citizens, but each has its own **jurisdiction** in legislation, taxation and administration.
3. Jurisdictions are specified in the **constitution** – existence and authority of each tier is constitutionally guaranteed.
4. Fundamental provisions **cannot be unilaterally changed** by one level; changes need consent of both.
5. **Courts** have power to interpret the constitution and powers of different levels – the highest court acts as an **umpire** in disputes.
6. **Sources of revenue** for each level are clearly specified to ensure financial autonomy.
7. Dual objectives: safeguard and promote **unity** of the country while accommodating **regional diversity**.

steps.title: Two kinds of federations
steps.body:
- **Coming together federations:** independent states come together on their own to form a bigger unit, pooling sovereignty and retaining identity to increase security – constituent states usually have **equal power** and are strong vis-à-vis the federal government. Examples: **USA, Switzerland, Australia**.
- **Holding together federations:** a large country decides to divide its power between constituent states and the national government – the central government tends to be **more powerful**; constituent units may have unequal powers (some get special powers). Examples: **India, Spain, Belgium**.

Belgium shifted from a unitary to a federal form (1993); Sri Lanka continues to be, for all practical purposes, a unitary system.

steps.title: Solved example: Distinguish federal and unitary systems (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Levels:** federal – two or more levels with own powers; unitary – one level, or sub-units subordinate.

**Step 2 – Constitution:** federal – powers guaranteed and cannot be changed unilaterally; unitary – centre can change powers.

**Step 3 – Example:** India/USA federal; Sri Lanka effectively unitary.

steps.title: Solved example: Why is India a holding-together federation? (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** A large, diverse country chose to divide power between the Union and states rather than independent states uniting.

**Step 2:** The Union is relatively more powerful, and some states have special provisions.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the USA holding-together – it is **coming together**.
- Saying in a federation the centre can order states freely – that describes a **unitary** system.

steps.title: Three-fold distribution of powers
steps.body:
The Constitution declared India a **Union of States**. It originally provided for two levels – the Union government and state governments; a third tier, **panchayats and municipalities**, was added later.

- **Union List:** subjects of national importance – **defence, foreign affairs, banking, communications, currency**. Only the Union government can make laws on them.
- **State List:** subjects of state and local importance – **police, trade, commerce, agriculture, irrigation**. Only state governments can make laws.
- **Concurrent List:** common interest to both – **education, forest, trade unions, marriage, adoption and succession**. Both can make laws; if there is a conflict, **Union law prevails**.
- **Residuary subjects** (not in any list, e.g. computer software) – the **Union government** has power to legislate.

Not all states have identical powers; some (e.g. several north-eastern states) enjoy special status under certain provisions. **Union Territories** (like Chandigarh, Lakshadweep, Delhi) are areas too small to be independent states or could not be merged; the Union government has special powers in running them.

steps.title: Safeguards of the federal structure
steps.body:
- Sharing of power cannot be changed by Parliament alone: changes need both Houses of Parliament with at least a **two-thirds majority**, and then ratification by the legislatures of **at least half of the total states**.
- The **judiciary** (High Courts and Supreme Court) supervises the implementation of constitutional provisions; in disputes the Supreme Court decides.
- Both levels can **raise resources** by levying taxes as specified in the Constitution.

**Step 2:** In case of conflict, the **Union law prevails**.

steps.body:
- Putting police on the Union List – it is a **State** subject.
- Saying residuary powers go to states – they go to the **Union**.
- Forgetting the ratification requirement: **at least half the states**.

steps.title: Linguistic states and language policy
steps.body:
- **Linguistic states:** after 1947 many old state boundaries were changed to ensure people speaking the same language lived in the same state; some states were created on culture, ethnicity or geography (e.g. Nagaland, Uttarakhand, Jharkhand). Initially leaders feared disintegration; experience shows formation of linguistic states made the country more united and administration easier.
- **Language policy:** the Constitution did not give **national language** status to any one language. **Hindi** was identified as the **official language**, but it is the mother tongue of only about **40%** of Indians (NCERT figure). Besides Hindi, **21 other languages** are recognised as **Scheduled Languages** (Eighth Schedule – total 22). A candidate in a Union government exam may choose any of these languages. States have their own official languages. The use of **English** for official purposes alongside Hindi continued after 1965 as non-Hindi states (e.g. Tamil Nadu) opposed its replacement. The Union government promotes Hindi but cannot impose it.

steps.title: Centre–state relations
steps.body: Restructuring centre–state relations strengthened federalism in practice. For a long time the same party ruled at the Centre and most states, so states did not exercise rights as autonomous units. When a different party ruled a state, the Centre sometimes misused the Constitution to dismiss state governments. After **1990** came the rise of **regional parties** and the beginning of the era of **coalition governments** at the Centre; no single party got a clear majority, so national parties had to enter alliances with regional parties, building a new culture of power sharing and respect for autonomy. A **Supreme Court judgement** made it difficult for the Centre to dismiss state governments arbitrarily.

steps.title: Solved example: How did linguistic states strengthen national unity? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** People speaking the same language could administer themselves in their own language – administration became easier.

**Step 2:** Regional aspirations were met within the Union, reducing resentment.

**Step 3:** Contrary to fears of break-up, India became more united.

steps.title: Solved example: Why did coalition politics strengthen federalism? (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** After 1990, no single party had a majority; national parties needed regional parties.

**Step 2:** This forced the Centre to respect state autonomy and share power.

steps.body:
- Writing that Hindi is India's **national language** – the Constitution gives no language that status; Hindi is the **official** language.
- Counting “22 languages besides Hindi” – it is **21 besides Hindi**, 22 in total.

steps.title: Why decentralisation and the 1992 amendment
steps.body:
**Decentralisation** is when power is taken away from Central and State governments and given to **local government**. Many problems are best settled locally; people know their needs; local participation builds democracy.

A major step was taken in **1992**, when the Constitution was amended (**73rd and 74th amendments**) to make the third tier more powerful and effective:
- It is **constitutionally mandatory to hold regular elections** to local government bodies.
- **Seats are reserved** in elected bodies and executive heads for **SCs, STs and OBCs**.
- At least **one-third of all positions are reserved for women**.
- An independent **State Election Commission** in each state conducts panchayat and municipal elections.
- State governments are required to **share some powers and revenue** with local bodies (nature varies by state).

steps.title: Structure of local government
steps.body:
**Rural (Panchayati Raj):**
- **Gram panchayat** – each village or group of villages; council of several ward members (**panch**) and a president (**sarpanch**), directly elected by all adults of the ward/village.
- **Gram sabha** – all voters in the village; meets at least twice or thrice a year to approve the annual budget and review the panchayat's performance.
- **Panchayat samiti** (block or mandal) – a few gram panchayats grouped; members elected by panchayat members of the area.
- **Zila (district) parishad** – all panchayat samitis of a district; most members elected; also includes Lok Sabha and MLA members of the district and some officials; its chairperson is the political head.

**Urban:** **municipalities** in towns and **municipal corporations** in big cities, both controlled by elected bodies of people's representatives. The **municipal chairperson** is political head of a municipality; in a corporation the officer is the **mayor**.

Result: about **36 lakh** elected representatives in panchayats and municipalities (NCERT figure) – the largest experiment in democracy. Problems: gram sabhas not held regularly; most state governments have not transferred significant powers or adequate resources.

steps.body:

**Step 2 – Gram panchayat:** elected council (panch + sarpanch) that is the decision-making body.

steps.body:
- Saying the panchayat samiti is at the district level – it is at the **block/mandal** level; the **zila parishad** is at the district level.
- Calling the head of a municipal corporation “sarpanch” – it is the **mayor**.
- Writing one-half reservation for women – the Constitution requires **at least one-third**.

steps.title: Public–private division
steps.body:
Gender division is a form of hierarchical social division based on social expectations and stereotypes, not on biology. The **sexual division of labour**: a system in which all work inside the home is done by women of the family or organised by them through domestic helpers, while men are expected to work outside. Women do domestic work and also much paid work outside, but their work is often not valued or recognised. Their share in public life, especially politics, was minimal in most societies.

**Feminist movements** – radical women's movements that aim at equality in personal and family life and public affairs – agitated for equal voting rights, educational and career opportunities, and greater participation. In Scandinavian countries such as Sweden, Norway and Finland, participation of women in public life is very high.

steps.title: Discrimination in India
steps.body:
- **Literacy:** the literacy rate among women is lower than among men (NCERT figures show a gap of around 20 percentage points); a smaller proportion of girls go for higher studies – parents prefer to spend on boys' education.
- **Work and wages:** women work more hours than men on average, but much of their work is unpaid and unvalued. The **Equal Remuneration Act, 1976** provides that equal wages should be paid for equal work, yet women are often paid less than men.
- **Sex-selective abortion:** many parents prefer sons, leading to a decline in the **child sex ratio** (number of girl children per thousand boys) in many states.
- **Safety:** harassment, exploitation and violence in urban areas and at home make women feel unsafe.

steps.title: Women's political representation
steps.body:
- The share of women in the **Lok Sabha** has been low; it touched **14.36%** for the first time in **2019** (NCERT figure). Their share in state assemblies is lower (under 5% in many). In the Union Council of Ministers women have been few.
- Since **1992**, **one-third of seats in panchayats and municipalities** are reserved for women; there are more than 10 lakh elected women representatives in rural and urban local bodies (NCERT figure).
- Women's organisations long demanded similar reservation in legislatures. In **2023**, Parliament passed the **Constitution (106th Amendment) Act – Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam**, which reserves **one-third of seats** in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies for women; it will take effect after the delimitation that follows the next census.

steps.title: Solved example: What is the sexual division of labour? Why is it unfair? (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Meaning:** housework and child-rearing are seen as women's work; outside paid work as men's.

**Step 2 – Unfairness:** women's domestic work is unpaid and unrecognised; they also work outside and end up working more hours.

**Step 3 – Effect:** it limits women's role in public life and politics.

steps.title: Solved example: Give three forms of discrimination against women in India (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – Education:** lower literacy and fewer girls in higher studies.

**Step 2 – Wages:** paid less than men for equal work despite the Equal Remuneration Act 1976.

**Step 3 – Sex ratio:** son preference and sex-selective abortion lower the child sex ratio.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying gender division is biological – it is based on **social expectations and stereotypes**.
- Writing that women already have one-third reservation in Lok Sabha **now** – the 2023 Act takes effect only **after delimitation following the next census**.
- Confusing child sex ratio (girls per 1,000 boys) with literacy.

steps.title: Religion in politics
steps.body:
Religious differences can be expressed in politics. Gandhi said religion can never be separated from politics – by religion he meant moral values that inform all religions. People should be able to express their needs, interests and demands as members of a religious community; those in political power should be able to regulate the practice of religion to prevent discrimination and oppression. Problems begin when religion is seen as the basis of the nation.

**Communalism:** politics in which one religion is presented as superior, followers of one religion are seen as one community with the same interests, which are opposed to those of other religions; it uses state power to establish the domination of one religious group.

**Forms of communalism:**
1. **Everyday beliefs** – religious prejudices, stereotypes of religious communities, belief in the superiority of one's religion.
2. **Majoritarian dominance / separate political unit** – the majority community seeks to dominate; the minority may want a separate political unit.
3. **Political mobilisation on religious lines** – sacred symbols, religious leaders, emotional appeal to bring followers together in politics.
4. **Communal violence, riots and massacres** – India and Pakistan suffered some of the worst at the time of Partition.

steps.title: Secular state
steps.body:
Communalism was and is one of the major challenges to democracy in India. The makers of the Constitution chose a **secular state**:
- There is **no official religion** for the Indian state (unlike Buddhism in Sri Lanka, Islam in Pakistan or Christianity in England).
- The Constitution provides **freedom to profess, practise and propagate any religion**, or not to follow any.
- It **prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion**.
- It allows the state to **intervene in religious matters to ensure equality** within religious communities – e.g. it **bans untouchability**.

Secularism is not just an ideology of some parties; it is one of the foundations of the country.

steps.title: Solved example: Identify the form of communalism (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1 – “Our religion is better than theirs”:** everyday belief.

**Step 2 – A party asks for votes using religious symbols:** political mobilisation on religious lines.

**Step 3 – Riots after a rumour:** communal violence.

steps.title: Solved example: Name four features of India's secular Constitution (4 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** No official religion.

**Step 2:** Freedom to profess, practise and propagate any religion.

**Step 3:** Prohibits discrimination based on religion.

**Step 4:** State may intervene in religious matters to ensure equality (e.g. ban on untouchability).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying secularism means the state has nothing to do with religion – Indian secularism allows the state to **intervene to ensure equality**.
- Equating all religious expression in politics with communalism – communalism means using religion to claim superiority or domination.

steps.title: Caste inequalities
steps.body:
In most societies occupations pass from one generation to another; caste is an extreme form of this, where members of the same caste group form a social community practising the same or similar occupation, marry within the group and do not eat with other caste groups. **Untouchability** was an extreme form of discrimination.

Partly due to efforts of reformers (**Jotiba Phule, Gandhi, B.R. Ambedkar, Periyar Ramaswami Naicker**) and socio-economic changes – **urbanisation, growth of literacy and education, occupational mobility, weakening of landlords** – caste hierarchy has broken down considerably. The Constitution **prohibits caste-based discrimination**. Yet caste continues to be closely linked to economic status (upper castes generally better off; Dalits and Adivasis worse off) and many still marry within caste.

steps.title: Caste in politics and politics in caste
steps.body:
**Caste in politics:**
- Parties choose candidates keeping in mind the caste composition of the electorate.
- Parties and candidates appeal to caste sentiment; some parties are known to favour some castes.
- **Universal adult franchise** and one-person-one-vote made leaders mobilise votes, bringing new consciousness among castes previously treated as inferior.

**But elections are not only about caste:** no parliamentary constituency has a clear majority of one single caste; no party wins the votes of all members of a caste; many voters vote on issues; ruling parties and sitting MPs often lose; voters assess performance.

**Politics in caste:** each caste group tries to become bigger by incorporating neighbouring castes or sub-castes; caste groups enter coalitions with other castes; new kinds of groups emerge like “backward” and “forward” castes. Caste politics has helped Dalits and OBCs gain better access to decision-making, but exclusive attention to caste can divert from issues like poverty and corruption, and can lead to tensions and violence.

steps.title: Solved example: “Elections in India are not only about caste.” Give three reasons (3 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** No constituency has a clear majority of one caste – candidates need support from many groups.

**Step 2:** No party gets all the votes of a caste; voters often have several candidates from their caste.

**Step 3:** Ruling parties and sitting MPs often lose – voters judge performance and issues.

steps.title: Solved example: How does politics influence caste? (2 marks)
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Caste groups expand by including neighbouring sub-castes and form coalitions.

**Step 2:** New categories like “backward” and “forward” emerge in political discourse.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying caste has vanished – it persists, especially in marriage and economic status.
- Assuming every voter votes by caste – voters consider performance and issues too.
